figures.point: A missing lower first molar is replaced by a false tooth held by crowns on the two neighbouring teeth.

figures.point: An onlay rebuilds the cusps of a molar from a lab-made piece bonded into a shallow preparation, keeping more tooth than a crown.

Upper central incisor
figures.point: Shape of the upper central incisor: wide labial face, cingulum, single conical root, pulp horns under the incisal edge.

figures.title: Upper canine, the longest root
figures.point: The canine has the longest root in the mouth and a single pointed cusp; that is why it anchors the arch.

figures.title: Upper lateral incisor
figures.point: The lateral incisor is a smaller central with a narrower root, often with a deep palatal pit.

figures.title: Upper first premolar, two roots
figures.point: The upper first premolar usually has two roots (buccal and palatal) and two canals, unlike the lower premolars.

figures.title: Lower first premolar
figures.point: The lower first premolar has one root, a large buccal cusp and a tiny lingual cusp; a second canal hides in about a quarter.

figures.title: Upper first molar, three roots
figures.point: The upper first molar has three roots (mesiobuccal, distobuccal, palatal) and the oblique ridge on its crown.

figures.title: Lower incisors
figures.point: Lower incisors are the smallest teeth: narrow crowns and flat roots that often hide a second, lingual canal.

figures.title: Cusps and grooves of a molar
figures.point: The chewing surface of a lower first molar: five cusps, central fossa and the grooves where decay starts.

figures.title: What holds a tooth in
figures.point: A tooth hangs in its socket by the periodontal ligament between cementum and bone, sealed at the top by gum.

figures.title: The 20 baby teeth
figures.point: Children have 20 primary teeth, 10 per jaw, with no premolars, lettered A to T or numbered 51 to 85.

figures.title: Baby molar vs adult molar
figures.point: Primary molars have thin enamel, large pulp horns close to the surface and flared roots that cradle the premolar below.

figures.title: How many canals in a root
figures.point: One root can hold one or two canals that split and join in a few typical patterns (Vertucci types).

figures.title: C-shaped canal in a lower second molar
figures.point: Fused roots of a lower second molar can hold one C-shaped canal instead of separate canals.

figures.title: Upper molar roots and the sinus
figures.point: Upper molar roots often sit right under the sinus floor, so tooth pain and sinus pain get confused.

figures.title: The nerve canal in the lower jaw
figures.point: The inferior alveolar nerve runs in a canal under the lower molar roots and exits at the mental foramen below the premolars.

figures.title: When adult teeth come in
figures.point: Adult teeth erupt in a typical order from about age 6 (first molars) to 12 (second molars), third molars later.
queries: when do adult teeth come in

figures.title: The pulp shrinks with age
figures.point: Secondary dentin narrows the pulp chamber and canals over a lifetime, so older teeth are harder to treat and less sensitive.

figures.title: Upper and lower teeth together
figures.point: 32 adult teeth in two arches: how the upper arch overlaps the lower when you bite.

figures.title: How a cavity reaches the nerve
figures.point: Decay goes through enamel, spreads in dentin and finally reaches the pulp; each stage needs a bigger treatment.
queries: does a cavity need a root canal

figures.title: Cavity between two teeth
figures.point: Decay starts just below the contact point where brushing cannot reach, which is why it shows on X-rays before you see it.

figures.title: Black's cavity classes
figures.point: G.V. Black's classes I to VI name a cavity by where it is: pits, proximal back, proximal front, incisal angle, cervical, cusp tips.

figures.title: Class I composite filling
figures.point: A small occlusal cavity is cleaned out, bonded and filled in cured layers of tooth-coloured composite.

figures.title: Bonding a chipped front tooth
figures.point: A chipped incisal corner is rebuilt with layered composite, shaped and polished to match.

figures.title: Filling at the gumline
figures.point: A notch at the gumline (class V) is filled with composite or glass ionomer after cleaning the root surface.

figures.title: Silver amalgam filling
figures.point: Amalgam needs an undercut box shape to hold mechanically, unlike bonded composite.

figures.title: Fissure sealant
figures.point: Thin resin flows into the deep grooves of a molar and seals them before decay can start.

figures.title: Cracked tooth
figures.point: A crack runs from the chewing surface toward the pulp; biting flexes it open, which causes sharp pain on release.

figures.title: Five kinds of tooth cracks
figures.point: Craze line, fractured cusp, cracked tooth, split tooth and vertical root fracture differ in where they start and how far they run.

figures.title: Why teeth are sensitive
figures.point: When gum recedes, open dentin tubules let cold move fluid toward the nerve, which you feel as a sharp twinge.

figures.title: Four kinds of tooth wear
figures.point: Erosion (acid), attrition (grinding), abrasion (brushing) and abfraction (flexing) leave different shapes of lost tooth.

figures.title: How an inlay fits
figures.point: An inlay is a lab-made filling that sits inside the cusps, cemented into a tapered cavity.

figures.title: Deep filling near the nerve
figures.point: In a deep cavity, a thin layer of affected dentin is left over the pulp and lined before filling, to avoid exposing the nerve.

figures.title: Rubber dam isolation
figures.point: A rubber sheet held by a clamp isolates the tooth so it stays dry and nothing falls into the throat.

figures.title: Decay under an old filling
figures.point: New decay starts at the edge of an old filling where a gap lets bacteria in, and spreads underneath.

figures.title: White spots on teeth
figures.point: Chalky white spots are early decay under an intact surface, often after braces, and can still remineralise.

figures.title: Why a toothache throbs
figures.point: Decay reaching the pulp inflames it; the swollen pulp is trapped in hard walls, which is why the pain throbs.

figures.title: Tooth abscess
figures.point: A dead pulp infects the bone at the root tip; pus may drain through a gum boil.

figures.title: Access cavity shapes
figures.point: Each tooth type has its own access outline, set by where its canal orifices are.

figures.title: Measuring working length
figures.point: Working length ends at the apical constriction, about 0.5 to 1 mm short of the radiographic apex.

figures.title: Filling the root canal
figures.point: Shaped canals are filled with gutta-percha and sealer to the working length, then sealed coronally.

figures.title: Direct pulp cap
figures.point: A small clean pulp exposure is covered with MTA or calcium silicate so the pulp can heal under a seal.

figures.title: Root canal on a front tooth
figures.point: A front tooth has one straight canal; access is from behind, through the palatal surface.

figures.title: Root canal on a premolar
figures.point: An upper first premolar has two canals, buccal and palatal, both shaped and filled.

figures.title: Redoing a failed root canal
figures.point: Old filling is removed, the missed or leaking canal cleaned and the tooth filled again.

figures.title: Apicoectomy
figures.point: Through a window in the bone, the infected root tip is cut off and sealed from below.

figures.title: Root resorption
figures.point: Resorption eats the root from inside (internal) or outside (external), with different shapes on X-ray.

figures.title: Vertical root fracture
figures.point: A crack along a root-filled root causes a narrow, deep pocket and a J-shaped bone loss; the tooth usually cannot be saved.

figures.title: Immature tooth with an open apex
figures.point: A young tooth has thin walls and a wide-open apex, so it needs apexification or regeneration instead of a normal root canal.

figures.title: Endo-perio lesion
figures.point: Infection from the pulp and from the gum pocket can meet along the root and join into one lesion.

figures.title: Plaque and tartar
figures.point: Soft plaque hardens into tartar above and below the gumline, where only a professional cleaning removes it.

figures.title: Deep cleaning
figures.point: A scaler goes into the pocket and removes tartar from the root, so the gum can heal back against it.

figures.title: Gum recession
figures.point: Gum and thin bone pull back from the root, exposing it; the tooth looks longer and gets sensitive.

figures.title: Gum graft
figures.point: Tissue from the palate is placed over the exposed root and covered with the gum flap.

figures.title: Horizontal vs vertical bone loss
figures.point: Bone can be lost evenly across teeth (horizontal) or in an angular defect beside one root (vertical).

figures.title: Furcation classes
figures.point: Bone loss between the roots of a molar is graded by how far a probe enters the furcation.

figures.title: Gum abscess
figures.point: Pus collects in a deep gum pocket beside a living tooth, unlike a tooth abscess at the root tip.

figures.title: Crown lengthening
figures.point: Gum and bone are moved down so a crown has enough healthy tooth above the bone to hold on to.

figures.title: Fixing a gummy smile
figures.point: Excess gum covering the front teeth is trimmed back to show their full crowns.

figures.title: Pocket reduction surgery
figures.point: The gum is lifted to clean the roots under direct view, then sutured lower to shrink the pocket.

figures.title: Regrowing lost bone
figures.point: A membrane over a filled bony defect keeps gum out so bone and ligament can regrow.

figures.title: Loose teeth and mobility grades
figures.point: With less bone holding the root, a tooth moves further; mobility is graded by how far.

figures.title: Black triangles between teeth
figures.point: When bone sits too far below the contact point, the papilla cannot fill the space and a dark triangle shows.

figures.title: Biologic width
figures.point: About 2 mm of soft tissue attaches the gum above the bone; a filling or crown margin placed into it causes inflammation.

figures.title: Implant or bridge?
figures.point: A bridge cuts down the two neighbours to hold a false tooth; an implant replaces the root and leaves them alone.

figures.title: Front tooth implant
figures.point: In the front, the implant sits slightly palatal and deep so thin labial bone and gum keep the tooth looking natural.

figures.title: All-on-4 full arch
figures.point: Four implants, the back two tilted, hold a full fixed arch of teeth.

figures.title: Snap-in implant denture
figures.point: Two implants in the lower jaw carry attachments that snap into a denture so it stops moving.

figures.title: Bone graft after extraction
figures.point: Filling the socket with graft right after extraction keeps the bone from collapsing before an implant.

figures.title: Sinus lift
figures.point: When the bone under the sinus is too thin, the sinus floor is lifted and grafted so an implant fits.

figures.title: Crestal sinus lift
figures.point: Through the implant site, osteotomes tap the sinus floor up a few millimetres before the implant goes in.

figures.title: Implant on extraction day
figures.point: The tooth is removed and the implant placed into the fresh socket, with graft in the gap.

figures.title: Screw- vs cement-retained crown
figures.point: A screw-retained crown can be taken off through an access hole; a cemented one has no hole but risks excess cement.

figures.title: How an implant fuses to bone
figures.point: Over about three to six months, new bone grows onto the implant surface and locks it in place.

figures.title: Implant-supported bridge
figures.point: Two implants can carry a three-tooth bridge, so three missing teeth do not need three implants.

figures.title: Building up a thin ridge
figures.point: Particulate graft under a membrane widens a thin ridge before an implant can go in.

figures.title: Peri-implantitis
figures.point: Infection around an implant destroys bone in a crater around its threads.

figures.title: Mini implant vs standard implant
figures.point: Mini implants under 3 mm wide fit narrow bone but carry less load than standard implants.

figures.title: Implant safety distances
figures.point: Keep at least 1.5 mm to a tooth, 3 mm between implants and about 2 mm above the nerve canal.

figures.title: Implant vs natural tooth
figures.point: A tooth floats on its ligament; an implant is fused to bone with no ligament, so it cannot move or feel pressure the same way.

figures.title: Crown materials compared
figures.point: Gold, metal-ceramic, zirconia and lithium disilicate crowns need different thicknesses and look different.

figures.title: Why a root canal tooth needs a crown
figures.point: Access and lost walls leave a hollow, brittle tooth; a crown wraps it so it does not split.
queries: do I need a crown after root canal

figures.title: What's under a crown
figures.point: A crown is a shell cemented over the shaved-down tooth; if it falls off, the stump underneath is still your tooth.

figures.title: Preparing a molar for a crown
figures.point: A molar is reduced occlusally then axially with a chamfer, then the crown seats on the prep.

figures.title: Maryland bridge
figures.point: A false tooth is held by thin wings bonded to the backs of the neighbours, with little or no drilling.

figures.title: Cantilever bridge
figures.point: A pontic hangs off one abutment only, which works for light-load spaces like a missing lateral incisor.

figures.title: A full smile of veneers
figures.point: Six to ten thin veneers on the front teeth change shape and shade of the whole smile.

figures.title: Temporary crown
figures.point: A temporary crown protects the prepared tooth and holds the space for the weeks until the final crown.

figures.title: Same-day crown
figures.point: The prep is scanned, the crown designed on screen and milled from a ceramic block in the office.

figures.title: Crown margin designs
figures.point: Chamfer, shoulder, knife edge and bevelled shoulder margins suit different crown materials.

figures.title: Decay under a crown
figures.point: Decay starts at the crown margin near the gum and spreads under the crown where it cannot be seen.

figures.title: Complete denture
figures.point: A full denture rests on the gums and is held by suction and muscles; the upper one covers the palate.

figures.title: Partial denture
figures.point: A metal frame with clasps and rests clips onto remaining teeth and carries replacement teeth.

figures.title: Flexible partial denture
figures.point: A flexible nylon base with gum-coloured clasps replaces a few teeth without metal.

figures.title: Flipper tooth
figures.point: A small acrylic plate carries one false tooth as a stopgap while an implant heals.

figures.title: Relining a loose denture
figures.point: Bone shrinks after extractions, so a gap opens under the denture; a reline fills it.

figures.title: Night guard
figures.point: A hard acrylic splint covers the upper teeth so grinding wears the guard instead of the teeth.

figures.title: Sports mouthguard
figures.point: A thick soft guard over the upper teeth spreads the force of a blow.

figures.title: Snoring and sleep apnea device
figures.point: Two linked splints hold the lower jaw forward, which pulls the tongue forward and opens the airway.

figures.title: Parts of a brace
figures.point: Each brace is a bracket bonded to the tooth, with the archwire held in its slot by a ligature.

figures.title: Rubber bands with braces
figures.point: Elastics hooked between upper and lower braces pull the jaws to fix how the bite meets.

figures.title: Palatal expander
figures.point: Turning the screw widens the upper jaw at the midpalatal suture in children.

figures.title: Types of retainers
figures.point: Clear, Hawley and bonded wire retainers all hold teeth after braces; teeth drift back without them.

figures.title: Angle's bite classes
figures.point: Class I, II and III are named by where the upper first molar sits against the lower one.

figures.title: Overbite vs overjet
figures.point: Overbite is how far upper teeth cover lower teeth vertically; overjet is how far they stick out in front.

figures.title: Underbite
figures.point: In an underbite the lower front teeth close in front of the upper ones, usually because the lower jaw is larger.

figures.title: Crossbite
figures.point: In a crossbite upper back teeth bite inside the lower ones, often because the upper jaw is narrow.

figures.title: Open bite
figures.point: In an open bite the front teeth do not meet when the back teeth close.

figures.title: Crowded teeth
figures.point: When teeth are wider than the arch, they overlap and rotate; space is gained by expansion, stripping or extraction.

figures.title: Gap between front teeth
figures.point: A gap between the upper central incisors often comes with a low frenum or small lateral teeth.

figures.title: Aligner attachments
figures.point: Small tooth-coloured bumps give the aligner something to push on so it can rotate and move teeth.

figures.title: Orthodontic mini-screw
figures.point: A temporary mini-screw between roots is a fixed anchor to pull teeth against.

figures.title: Braces behind the teeth
figures.point: Lingual brackets bond to the tongue side, so the braces are hidden from the front.

figures.title: Bringing down an impacted canine
figures.point: A stuck canine is uncovered, a bracket and chain bonded to it, and braces pull it into the arch.

figures.title: Wisdom tooth positions
figures.point: Impacted lower wisdom teeth are vertical, mesioangular, horizontal or distoangular; the angle decides how hard removal is.

figures.title: Simple tooth extraction
figures.point: The elevator loosens the tooth and forceps rock it out by stretching the socket.

figures.title: Surgical wisdom tooth removal
figures.point: Gum is opened, some bone removed and the tooth cut in pieces so it comes out without force on the jaw.

figures.title: Dry socket
figures.point: If the blood clot is lost from the socket, bare bone is exposed and it hurts a lot after a few days.

figures.title: How a socket heals
figures.point: Clot, then soft tissue, then new bone fill the socket over weeks to months.

figures.title: Where the numbing shot goes
figures.point: For lower teeth, the anaesthetic is placed near the nerve as it enters the jaw, numbing the teeth, lip and tongue on that side.

figures.title: Coronectomy
figures.point: When roots touch the nerve, only the crown is removed and the roots are left so the nerve is not injured.

figures.title: Tongue-tie and lip-tie release
figures.point: A tight frenum is cut so the tongue or lip moves freely.

figures.title: Lower jaw surgery
figures.point: In a split osteotomy, the lower jaw is cut behind the teeth and moved forward or back, then fixed with plates.

figures.title: Cyst around a wisdom tooth
figures.point: Fluid collects around the crown of an unerupted tooth and slowly expands the bone.

figures.title: Knocked-out tooth
figures.point: Put the tooth back in its socket fast, holding the crown not the root, because the ligament cells die when dry.
queries: what to do knocked out tooth

figures.title: Baby tooth pulpotomy
figures.point: In a baby molar, only the infected pulp in the crown is removed; the root pulp stays alive.

figures.title: Steel crown for a baby molar
figures.point: A preformed steel crown covers a badly decayed baby molar until it falls out naturally.

figures.title: Space maintainer
figures.point: After a baby molar is lost early, a band and loop holds the space so the adult tooth can come in.

figures.title: Baby bottle tooth decay
figures.point: Milk or juice at night pools on the upper front baby teeth, which decay first; the lower ones are shielded by the tongue.

figures.title: Teething: which teeth come first
figures.point: Lower central incisors usually break through the gum first, at around 6 to 10 months.

figures.title: Shark teeth in children
figures.point: Adult lower incisors often erupt behind baby teeth that have not fallen out yet; the tongue usually moves them forward.

figures.title: The jaw joint
figures.point: The condyle sits in its fossa with a disc between; on opening it rotates, then slides forward onto the eminence.

figures.title: How the jaw opens
figures.point: The first 20 to 25 mm of opening is rotation of the condyle; wider opening slides it forward onto the eminence.

figures.title: Clicking jaw: disc displacement
figures.point: The disc sits in front of the condyle when closed and pops back on as the mouth opens: that is the click.

figures.title: Teeth grinding
figures.point: Grinding loads teeth, muscles and joints far beyond chewing forces, which flattens teeth and tires the jaw.

figures.title: Canine guidance vs group function
figures.point: On a side movement, either the canines alone or several back teeth guide the jaw and keep the others apart.

figures.title: Jaw moving forward
figures.point: When the jaw protrudes, the incisors guide it and the back teeth separate (anterior guidance).

figures.title: How teeth whitening works
figures.point: Peroxide passes through enamel into dentin and breaks down the stain molecules that make teeth look yellow.

figures.title: Brushing at the gumline
figures.point: Angle bristles at 45 degrees into the gumline and use short strokes; that is where plaque builds up.

figures.title: How to floss
figures.point: Wrap the floss in a C around each tooth and slide it just under the gum, both sides of every contact.
